'''''Chaenorhinum minus''''', also known as '''small toadflax''' in Europe and '''dwarf snapdragon''' in the US and Canada, is a very diminutive member of the plant family [[Plantaginaceae]].<ref name=":0">[http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/small-toadflax NatureGate - Small Toadflax]</ref> It is native to continental [[Europe]].<ref name=":1">[https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/chaenorhinum-minus Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora]</ref>

==Description==
''Chaenorhinum minus'' differs from many toadflaxes in having alternate leaves growing singly. Its leaves and sepals are covered with glandular hairs. Leaves are glaucous and sepals are green or purple. Flowers vary from pale purple to white. It is an annual herb, with a maximum height of {{Convert|25|cm|abbr=on}}. It does not spread vegetatively.<ref name=":1" /> Flowering occurs June–July.<ref name=":0" />

==Taxonomy==
''Chaenorhinum minus'' was given the name ''Antirrhinum minus'' in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]]. The botanist [[René Louiche Desfontaines]] placed it in the genus ''[[Linaria]]'' in 1798 and finally it was moved to the genus ''[[Chaenorhinum]]'' in 1870 by [[Johan Lange]], giving the species its accepted name. Together with its genus it is classified in the family [[Plantaginaceae]].<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |date=2026 |id=801401-1 |title=''Chaenorhinum minus'' (L.) Lange |access-date=11 February 2026}}</ref>

==Habitat and distribution==
It is such a small plant that it relies upon disturbance to compete with other plants for light. Once a common weed in farmers' fields, it has suffered from agricultural intensification and is now mainly seen in gardens and around railways, as well as roadsides and industrial sites.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Its UK distribution shows it favours chalky soil.

This species is native to continental Europe, found mainly in south and central Europe, though it reaches as far north as Sweden. It is considered to have '[[archaeophyte]]' status in the [[United Kingdom]] ie. is thought to have been introduced many centuries ago.<ref name=":1" /> It has also been introduced to the US and Canada.<ref>[http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=CHMI USDA - Chaenorhinum minus]</ref>
